newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Jinro shares tumble as group seeks rescue.
newsitem.headline: Jinro shares tumble as group seeks rescue.

text.p: The troubled Jinro Group called for emergency loans from its major creditors on Thursday, a move that sent share prices of the group's four affiliates listed on the Seoul stock exchange tumbling.

Jinro, the nation's 19th largest conglomerate, or chaebol, asked for 500 billion won ($559.1 million) from the Commerical Bank of Korea and SEOULBANK to rescue its cash-short companies, said Jinro spokesman Chun Young-taek.
"We urgently need the money to pay back our debts," Chun said.
The group, with 22 affiliates under its wing, was suffering from 2.8 trillion won in debt as of Thursday, another Jinro spokesman said.
"The appeal to the banks mirrors how difficult the group's financial status is," said analyst Lee Hee-myong of Samsung Securities. "It takes its toll on Jinro shares."
Group flagship Jinro Ltd, a leading distilled spirit producer, went limit-down 800 won to close at 9,600.
Both Jinro General Foods and Jinro Industries also hit their daily lower limits, shedding 420 won and 500 won to 4,880 and 5,760.
Kumbi, a glass bottle manufacturer, lost 800 won to 32,000.
Analysts forecast the battering of Jinro shares would continue until the companies were granted emergency loans.
Jinro announced on Monday it would sell off unprofitable business lines and other assets because of financial pressures. The group hoped to generate 1.2 trillion won by 1998.
Chun denied local reports that the sale of idle lands in Seoul to a Hong Kong company, Jesmond Korea, was part of its restructuring plan.
He said Jinro sold the real estate for 145.6 billion won last December after dropping plans to build a hotel.
"But investors are fearing the possibility of Jinro's default as they believe the group is unlikely to find buyers soon," analyst Hwang Chang-joong of LG Securities.

Analysts said Jinro's bid to mobilise more cash by selling assets would likely fall short as the group would probably have trouble getting the price it wanted. South Korea has experienced asset deflation on falling real estate prices.
Jinro has scheduled a meeting for possible buyers on Friday to give details of its sales plans.
About 300 people are expected to participate, including top conglomerates such as Hyundai, Samsung and LG groups.
"We are expecting a committee established by financial institutions will come up with some measures to finance Jinro on Monday," Chun said.

The committee, which will include local banks, merchant banking corporations, securities houses and life insurers, will screen financially troubled companies and decide whether they will extend fresh loans. It will begin work from next Monday.
Analysts, questioning how effective the committee could be, said non-banking financial institutions appeared reluctant to join the group.

Financial institutions have balked at extending fresh loans to companies rumoured to be experiencing serious liquidity problems, following the recent collapse of the flagships of the Hanbo and Sammi groups.
"The Jinro problem reminded investors of the nightmare of Sammi's failure as the trouble in the steelmaker surfaced five years ago," Lee said.
(Conversion $1 = 894.30)
